tool.name: DuckDB
tool.tagline: In-process analytical SQL database for files, DataFrames and laptops
tool.description: DuckDB is an embedded, columnar SQL database built for analytics: it runs inside your Python process, CLI or app with no server, and queries CSV, Parquet, JSON and DataFrames directly. It is the fastest way to do serious SQL analysis on a single machine, from a few megabytes to hundreds of gigabytes. Learn it to replace slow scripts and heavy clusters for everyday data work.

glossary.def: Running inside your own program as a library, instead of as a separate server program that your program connects to.
A command starting with a dot, such as .tables or .quit, that the DuckDB command-line program handles itself instead of running it as SQL.
A function used in FROM as if it were a table, such as read_csv('file.csv') or range(10).
Your program's open link to one database, through which it sends queries. Close it when you are done.
In DuckDB's Python library, a query that is ready but hasn't run yet. It runs when you fetch its rows, print it or convert it.
A placeholder such as ? in SQL text whose value is passed separately, so the value can never be mistaken for SQL.
A table held in a program's memory, with named columns, made by Python libraries such as pandas or Polars.
A standard way to hold tables in memory column by column, so different programs and libraries can share data without converting it.
DuckDB's fallback when a table name isn't found: it looks for a Python variable with that name, such as a DataFrame, and reads it as a table.
The part of DuckDB's read_csv that reads a sample of a CSV file and guesses its delimiter, header, quoting and column types.
Storing a table's files in folders named column=value, such as year=2025/, so a filter on that column can skip whole folders.
A block of many rows inside a Parquet or DuckDB file, with each column stored separately and min/max values recorded, so whole blocks can be skipped.
Reading only the columns a query actually uses, straight from the file, instead of reading every column and dropping some later.
Applying a query's WHERE conditions as early as possible, ideally while reading the file, so data that can't match is never loaded.
A join that matches each row to the closest earlier (or equal) row in another table, such as the latest price at the time of a trade.
A DuckDB clause that filters rows by the result of a window function, the way HAVING filters by the result of an aggregate.
In DuckDB, an add-on package of features (such as reading from S3 or PostgreSQL) installed with INSTALL and switched on with LOAD.
In DuckDB's engine, a chunk of up to 2,048 values from one column that each query step processes in one go.
DuckDB's way of sharing work between threads: the input is cut into small chunks (morsels) and each thread takes the next free one when it finishes.
Writing part of a query's in-between data to disk when it no longer fits in the memory limit, so the query can still finish, more slowly.
The smallest and largest value DuckDB records for each chunk of a column, so a filter can skip chunks whose range can't match.
Storing each distinct value of a column once and replacing every occurrence with a small number pointing to it.
The tree-shaped index DuckDB builds for PRIMARY KEY and UNIQUE constraints; it speeds up looking up single rows.
In a hash join, the input that is loaded into the in-memory lookup table; the other input is then checked against it row by row.
A query step for ORDER BY ... LIMIT n that keeps only the best n rows seen so far instead of sorting all rows.

concepts.name: What DuckDB is
concepts.summary: A SQL database for analysis that runs inside your own program: no server to set up, and very fast on a single computer.
concepts.why: Knowing where DuckDB fits tells you when to reach for it instead of a spreadsheet, SQLite or a big shared database server.
concepts.body:
Most databases you have met, like PostgreSQL, are servers: a separate program runs all the time and clients connect to it. **DuckDB** is different. It runs **in-process**: it is a **library**, a bundle of ready-made code that your own program loads and uses, the way SQLite is. There is no server to install and no user accounts to set up.

You can use DuckDB from several places: the `duckdb` program you type SQL into (next lesson), or from inside programs written in Python, R, Java and other languages. In Python, a popular programming language, it takes one install command, `pip install duckdb`.

SQLite is built for many small reads and writes of single rows, the kind an app does all day: that work is called **OLTP** (online transaction processing). DuckDB is built for **OLAP** (online analytical processing): queries that scan and total millions of rows.

Two design choices make it fast at that. It stores data column by column (**columnar storage**), so a query reads only the columns it uses. And it works on chunks of about two thousand values at once instead of one value at a time (**vectorized** execution).

It also uses the whole **CPU**, the chip that runs programs. A CPU has several **CPU cores**, and each core can work on its own share of the data at the same moment.

Typical uses:

- exploring data files without loading them anywhere first, such as **CSV** (a text file holding a table, with commas between the columns) or **Parquet** (a compact file that stores a table column by column)
- running SQL over tables a Python program already holds (a later lesson)
- small data-cleaning jobs and tests on your own computer
- adding fast analysis to an app

Its SQL dialect is close to PostgreSQL's, plus many conveniences, so the SQL you know works. A DuckDB database is either **in-memory**, kept only in the computer's **memory** (its fast working storage, wiped when your program ends), or saved in a single `.duckdb` file that stays.

DuckDB is not a replacement for PostgreSQL behind a website. Only one program at a time can open a database file for writing, and DuckDB is tuned for big scans, not for thousands of users making small changes at once.
concepts.code:
-- Type these into the duckdb program (next lesson),
-- or run them from Python with duckdb.sql("...")
SELECT 42 AS answer, version() AS v;     -- 42 | v1.5.x

-- range(N) is a built-in table of the numbers 0 to N-1,
-- in a column called range. Count and average ten million of them
-- in well under a second:
SELECT count(*) AS n, avg(range) AS mean
FROM range(10000000);                    -- 10000000 | 4999999.5
takeaways: DuckDB is a database that runs inside your program: a library, not a server
Columnar, vectorized and using every CPU core, so big scans and totals are fast
Use it for analysis on one computer, not as the database behind a busy app
pitfalls: Expecting several programs to write to the same database file at once; DuckDB allows only one writer.

quiz.q: Which workload is DuckDB designed for?
options: Many small single-row updates from a busy website
Scanning and aggregating large tables on one machine
Remembering which users are logged in to a website
Searching the words of millions of documents
quiz.explain: DuckDB is an OLAP engine built for big scans, joins and totals.

options: It runs as a library inside your application, with no separate server
It needs a group of separate helper servers
It can only run inside a browser
It starts a hidden database server the first time you use it
quiz.explain: Like SQLite, DuckDB is a library loaded into your program and runs inside it.

concepts.name: CLI, files and persistence
concepts.summary: Type SQL into the duckdb program, keep your work in a .duckdb file, and create tables that are still there next time.
concepts.why: Choosing an in-memory or a file-backed database decides whether your work is kept and whether others can open it.
concepts.body:
The quickest way to try DuckDB is its **CLI** (command-line interface): a program you start by typing its name in a **terminal**, the text window where you type commands (Terminal on a Mac, PowerShell on Windows). Run `duckdb` to start with an in-memory database, or `duckdb analytics.duckdb` to open that database file, creating it if needed.

The file is laid out the same way everywhere, so the same file can be opened later from Python with `duckdb.connect("analytics.duckdb")`, or from R, Java and other languages.

In the CLI you type SQL ending in `;`, plus **dot commands**: short commands starting with a dot that the CLI handles itself.

- `.tables` lists tables, `.schema` shows the `CREATE TABLE` statements behind them
- `.mode` changes how results are printed (`duckbox` by default, `csv`, `markdown`, `line`, ...)
- `.timer on` prints how long each query took
- `.read script.sql` runs the SQL saved in a file; `.quit` exits

Tables are created with ordinary SQL. `CREATE TABLE t AS SELECT ...` (often shortened to CTAS) saves the result of a query, or the contents of a file, as a new table.

In a file-backed database everything you create is saved automatically; there is no separate save step. Data kept like this, so that it survives the program ending, is called **persistent**. Once a transaction commits, its changes are safe even if the computer crashes.

You can also `ATTACH` more database files and use their tables with `db_name.table` names, so copying data between files is a single `INSERT ... SELECT`.

Since version 1.0, newer DuckDB versions can always read database files written by older ones.
takeaways: `duckdb file.duckdb` opens or creates a persistent single-file database
No file name means in-memory: the data is lost on exit
`CREATE TABLE ... AS SELECT` saves query results and files as tables
`ATTACH` lets you work with several database files at once
pitfalls: Forgetting the file name and losing an afternoon of work in an in-memory database.

quiz.q: You run `duckdb` with no arguments, create tables and quit. What happens to them?
options: They are saved to duckdb.db in the current folder
DuckDB refuses to create tables without a file
They are saved to your home folder
They are lost, because the session was in-memory
quiz.explain: Without a file argument the CLI uses an in-memory database that disappears when it exits.

concepts.name: Querying files directly
concepts.summary: Run SQL straight over CSV, Parquet and JSON files by putting the path in the FROM clause.
concepts.why: This is DuckDB's best-loved feature: answer questions about data files without loading them into a table first.
concepts.body:
DuckDB treats a file's name as a table. Write `SELECT * FROM 'sales.csv'` and it works out the format from the end of the name (`.csv`), guesses the column names and types, and reads through the file as the query runs. The same works for `.parquet` and `.json` files, and for zipped files like `.csv.gz`.

**JSON** files hold records written as names and values inside curly braces, like `{"region": "north", "amount": 10}`. DuckDB turns each name into a column.

Behind that shortcut are **table functions**: functions you use in `FROM` as if they were tables. Call them yourself when you need options: `read_csv`, `read_parquet` and `read_json`. A few patterns you will use daily:

- `DESCRIBE SELECT * FROM 'file.parquet'` shows the column names and types DuckDB guessed
- `SUMMARIZE 'file.csv'` prints the min, max, number of distinct values, nulls and more for each column
- `CREATE TABLE t AS FROM 'file.csv'` loads a file into a table once, if you will query it many times (in DuckDB, `FROM x` alone means `SELECT * FROM x`)

Querying files in place is great for exploring, but each query reads the file again. A CSV file is just text, so DuckDB must read and convert all of it every time.

Parquet stores each column separately and **compressed** (packed to take less space, like a zip file), so DuckDB reads only the columns a query needs. If you run many queries over a big CSV, load it into a table or convert it to Parquet first.

File names are looked up starting from the folder you started DuckDB in. Web addresses work too: `FROM 'https://example.com/data.csv'` downloads the file as it reads, using an add-on called `httpfs` that DuckDB loads automatically in most installations.
takeaways: A quoted file name in FROM is a table; the format comes from the end of the name
`read_csv`, `read_parquet`, `read_json` take options when the guesses are not enough
`DESCRIBE` and `SUMMARIZE` give a fast first look at an unknown file
pitfalls: Querying a huge CSV over and over instead of loading it into a table or converting it to Parquet once.

quiz.q: Why is querying one column of a Parquet file usually much faster than the same query on a CSV?
options: DuckDB keeps Parquet files in memory forever
CSV files can only be read by one CPU core
Parquet is columnar, so only the needed columns are read and unpacked
Parquet files are always smaller than 1 MB
quiz.explain: Parquet stores each column separately, so DuckDB skips the columns the query does not use.

concepts.name: The Python API
concepts.summary: Run queries from Python with duckdb.sql or a connection, pass values in safely, and get the results back as Python values.
concepts.why: Most people use DuckDB from Python programs, so this is the everyday way in.
concepts.body:
Python is a popular programming language and DuckDB's most common home. After `pip install duckdb` (pip installs Python add-ons), a program loads DuckDB with the line `import duckdb`. Then there are two ways in:

- `duckdb.sql(query)` runs SQL on a shared, ready-made in-memory database. Handy for quick experiments.
- `con = duckdb.connect("file.duckdb")` (or `connect()` for in-memory) gives you a **connection**: your own handle to one database, stored here under the name `con`. Use this in real programs. Close it with `con.close()`, or open it in a `with` block, which closes it for you when the block ends.

`sql()` returns a **relation**: a query that is ready but hasn't run yet. Nothing runs until you print it or fetch its rows; this wait-until-needed style is called **lazy** evaluation. Relations can be queried again, so you can build a query step by step.

Fetching gives you Python values: `fetchall()` returns a list of rows, `fetchone()` a single row, and `.show()` prints a table. Each row is a **tuple**, Python's fixed group of values in parentheses, like `('Ann', 34)`.

`con.execute(query, values)` runs a statement right away. Mark the places for values with `?` (or `$name`) and pass the values separately as a list; these placeholders are **query parameters**.

Never paste values into the SQL text yourself. A name like O'Brien breaks the quotes, and text typed by a stranger could change what your SQL does: an **injection attack**.

`executemany` runs one statement once for each row of values, but for loading lots of data it is far faster to insert from a file or from data you already hold.

A program can do several things at the same time in separate **threads**. One connection must not be used by several threads at once; give each thread its own `con.cursor()`, a second connection to the same database.
concepts.code:
import duckdb

with duckdb.connect() as con:            # in-memory database, closed at the end
    con.execute("CREATE TABLE users (id INT, name TEXT, age INT)")
    con.executemany("INSERT INTO users VALUES (?, ?, ?)",
                    [(1, "Ann", 34), (2, "Bob", 19), (3, "Cy", 52)])

    # ? is filled in with 30, safely
    rows = con.execute("SELECT name FROM users WHERE age > ? ORDER BY name",
                       [30]).fetchall()
    print(rows)                          # [('Ann',), ('Cy',)]

    rel = con.sql("SELECT avg(age) AS avg_age FROM users")   # not run yet
    print(rel.fetchone())                # (35.0,)
takeaways: `duckdb.sql` uses a shared in-memory database; `duckdb.connect` gives you your own
Relations run only when fetched or shown
Pass values as query parameters (`?` or `$name`), never by pasting them into the SQL text
Give each thread its own `con.cursor()`
pitfalls: Pasting values typed by users into the SQL text (for example with Python's f"..." strings), which breaks on quotes and allows injection attacks.

quiz.q: What does `duckdb.sql('SELECT 1')` return before you call fetchall()?
quiz.explain: sql() returns a relation, which runs only when you fetch, show or convert it.

concepts.name: Friendly SQL extensions
concepts.summary: Write shorter queries with GROUP BY ALL, SELECT * EXCLUDE/REPLACE, FROM-first queries and COLUMNS().
concepts.why: These shortcuts remove most of the repetitive typing in analysis SQL, and nearly all DuckDB code uses them.
concepts.body:
DuckDB keeps standard SQL working but adds conveniences that make exploratory queries much shorter:

- `GROUP BY ALL` groups by every non-aggregated column in the SELECT list, so you never repeat column lists. `ORDER BY ALL` sorts by every column left to right.
- `SELECT * EXCLUDE (a, b)` returns all columns except some; `SELECT * REPLACE (round(price, 2) AS price)` swaps an expression in place of a column.
- **FROM-first**: `FROM tbl` alone means `SELECT * FROM tbl`, and `FROM tbl SELECT x` is allowed.
- `COLUMNS(* EXCLUDE id)` expands to many columns, so `SELECT max(COLUMNS(*))` aggregates each column. `COLUMNS('price_.*')` picks the columns whose names match a text pattern (a regular expression).
- Column aliases can be reused later in the same SELECT and in WHERE and GROUP BY.
- `count()` without arguments, trailing commas in lists, and `LIMIT 10%` are accepted.

Other quality-of-life features include `UNION BY NAME` (match columns by name not position), `INSERT INTO t BY NAME`, and taking part of a string with `'hello'[1:3]` (gives `'hel'`).

These are DuckDB-specific: if a query must also run on PostgreSQL or another database, stick to standard SQL there. For exploring data and one-off work, they make SQL far less tedious.
concepts.code:
import duckdb

duckdb.sql("""
    CREATE TABLE orders AS SELECT * FROM (VALUES
        ('north', 'pen', 2, 1.5::DOUBLE), ('north', 'book', 1, 12.0),
        ('south', 'pen', 5, 1.5)) t(region, item, qty, price)
""")
print(duckdb.sql("""
    SELECT region, item, sum(qty * price) AS revenue
    FROM orders GROUP BY ALL ORDER BY ALL
""").fetchall())
# [('north', 'book', 12.0), ('north', 'pen', 3.0), ('south', 'pen', 7.5)]

print(duckdb.sql("SELECT * EXCLUDE (price) FROM orders LIMIT 1").columns)
# ['region', 'item', 'qty']
print(duckdb.sql("SELECT max(COLUMNS(* EXCLUDE (region, item))) FROM orders").fetchall())
# [(5, 12.0)]
takeaways: `GROUP BY ALL` / `ORDER BY ALL` remove repeated column lists
`* EXCLUDE` and `* REPLACE` reshape tables with many columns quickly
`COLUMNS(...)` applies one expression to many columns
FROM-first queries like `FROM t` are valid
pitfalls: Copying DuckDB-only shortcuts into queries that also have to run on another database.

quiz.q: Given SELECT city, year, sum(sales) FROM t GROUP BY ALL, what does it group by?
quiz.explain: GROUP BY ALL groups by all SELECT expressions that are not aggregates: city and year.

concepts.name: Reading messy CSV files
concepts.summary: Control how read_csv reads a file: delimiters, headers, types, dates and bad rows.
concepts.why: Real CSV files are rarely clean, and knowing the options turns a failing load into a one-line fix.
concepts.body:
`read_csv` runs a **sniffer**: it reads a sample of the file and guesses its layout. That covers the **delimiter** (the character between columns, such as a comma or semicolon), the quote character, the character used to mark a quote inside a value, whether the first line holds the column names, and each column's type.

The sniffer is usually right, but you can set any of these yourself:

- `delim`, `quote`, `escape`, `header` for the layout
- `columns = {'id': 'INTEGER', 'name': 'VARCHAR'}` to fix all names and types (no type guessing), or `types = {...}` to set only some
- `dateformat` / `timestampformat` for dates not written year-month-day, e.g. `'%d/%m/%Y'`
- `nullstr` for values like `'NA'` that should be NULL
- `all_varchar = true` to load everything as text and convert later
- `ignore_errors = true` to skip rows that can't be read, and `store_rejects = true` to keep them in a `reject_errors` table to look at
- `filename = true` adds a column with the name of the file each row came from

`sniff_csv('file.csv')` shows what the sniffer decided, which is the first thing to run when a load goes wrong. A common failure is a column guessed as integer from the sample that later contains text; increase `sample_size` (or `-1` for the whole file) or set the type yourself.

Reading CSV uses every CPU core and is fast, but it still has to turn text into values every time: convert large CSV files to Parquet once if they will be read again and again.
concepts.code:
import duckdb, os, tempfile

os.chdir(tempfile.mkdtemp())
with open("people.csv", "w") as f:
    f.write("name;born;score\nAnn;03/04/1990;7\nBob;NA;x\nCy;12/11/1985;9\n")

rel = duckdb.sql("""
    SELECT * FROM read_csv('people.csv', delim = ';', header = true,
        dateformat = '%d/%m/%Y', nullstr = 'NA',
        columns = {'name': 'VARCHAR', 'born': 'DATE', 'score': 'INTEGER'},
        ignore_errors = true)
""")
print(rel.fetchall())
# [('Ann', datetime.date(1990, 4, 3), 7), ('Cy', datetime.date(1985, 11, 12), 9)]
takeaways: The sniffer guesses the layout, header and types from a sample
`columns`/`types`, `dateformat` and `nullstr` fix most bad guesses
`ignore_errors` skips bad rows; `store_rejects` keeps them for review
Run `sniff_csv` to see what was detected
pitfalls: Silently dropping rows with `ignore_errors = true` and never checking how many were rejected.

quiz.q: A column was detected as BIGINT, but row 2 million contains 'n/a'. What is a good fix?
options: Delete the file and ask for JSON
Convert the file to Excel first
Use ORDER BY on the column
Set the column's type explicitly or set nullstr = 'n/a'
quiz.explain: Overriding the type or declaring the null marker fixes the mismatch the sample did not reveal.

concepts.name: Parquet, globs and partitions
concepts.summary: Query many files at once with glob patterns and Hive-partitioned folders, and let Parquet skip data.
concepts.why: Real data often comes as folders of many files; reading them as one table, and skipping the files a query doesn't need, is what makes DuckDB scale.
concepts.body:
A **glob pattern** in the file name reads many files as one table. `*` matches any part of a name, so `FROM 'logs/*.parquet'` reads every Parquet file in `logs`; `**` also looks inside every subfolder, as in `'data/**/*.csv'`. You can also pass a list: `read_parquet(['a.parquet', 'b.parquet'])`. Add `filename = true` to know which file each row came from, and `union_by_name = true` when files have different columns.

Big collections of raw data files kept for later analysis are called **data lakes**. Their files are usually split into folders by the value of a column, which is called **partitioning**. A common layout uses folders named `key=value`, e.g. `sales/year=2025/month=03/part-0.parquet`; it is known as **Hive partitioning**, after the tool that made it popular.

With `hive_partitioning = true` (switched on automatically for such paths) the folder keys become columns, and a filter like `WHERE year = 2025` skips whole folders without opening them.

**Parquet** makes queries cheap in two more ways. A Parquet file is split into **row groups** of many rows, each storing the smallest and largest value of every column.

- **projection pushdown**: only the columns in the query are read
- **filter pushdown**: row groups whose min/max values show they can't match a WHERE condition are skipped

`parquet_metadata('file.parquet')` and `parquet_schema(...)` show row groups, min/max values and types. All of this works the same for files on Amazon S3 (an online file store) or at web addresses, where skipping data also saves download time.
concepts.code:
import duckdb, os, tempfile

os.chdir(tempfile.mkdtemp())
duckdb.sql("""
    COPY (SELECT i AS id, i % 3 AS shop, 2024 + i % 2 AS year FROM range(12) t(i))
    TO 'sales' (FORMAT parquet, PARTITION_BY (year))
""")
print(sorted(os.listdir("sales")))       # ['year=2024', 'year=2025']

print(duckdb.sql("""
    SELECT year, count(*) AS n, sum(id) AS ids
    FROM read_parquet('sales/*/*.parquet', hive_partitioning = true)
    WHERE year = 2025 GROUP BY year
""").fetchall())                          # [(2025, 6, 36)]
takeaways: Glob patterns (`*`, `**`) and lists read many files as one table
Hive `key=value` folders become columns, and filters on them skip whole folders
Parquet reads only the needed columns and skips row groups using min/max values
pitfalls: Using thousands of tiny Parquet files: the fixed cost of opening each file dominates. Aim for files of tens to hundreds of megabytes.

quiz.q: With files under sales/year=2024/ and sales/year=2025/, what does WHERE year = 2025 let DuckDB do?
options: Nothing special; it reads every file
quiz.explain: Hive partition values come from folder names, so folders that can't match are skipped before reading.

concepts.name: Exporting with COPY
concepts.summary: Write tables and query results to Parquet, CSV or JSON, optionally partitioned, with COPY ... TO.
concepts.why: Converting and exporting data is half of most data jobs, and DuckDB does it in one statement.
concepts.body:
`COPY ... TO` writes a table or the result of any query to a file:

```sql
COPY (SELECT * FROM events WHERE ok) TO 'events.parquet' (FORMAT parquet);
```

The format comes from the end of the file name, or is set with `FORMAT`. Useful options:

- Parquet: `COMPRESSION zstd` (the default is snappy), `ROW_GROUP_SIZE`
- CSV: `HEADER`, `DELIMITER`
- `PARTITION_BY (col, ...)` writes a Hive-style folder tree, one subfolder per value
- `OVERWRITE_OR_IGNORE` / `OVERWRITE` control what happens if the target folder exists
- `PER_THREAD_OUTPUT` writes several files at once, one per CPU core working on the export, for maximum speed

The reverse direction, `COPY tbl FROM 'file.csv'`, appends a file into an existing table, though `INSERT INTO tbl SELECT * FROM 'file.csv'` is more flexible.

A common one-liner is CSV to Parquet conversion: `COPY (FROM 'raw.csv') TO 'clean.parquet'`. To move an entire database, `EXPORT DATABASE 'dir'` writes every table plus a file of the `CREATE` statements, and `IMPORT DATABASE 'dir'` rebuilds it.

Sort data by a frequently filtered column before writing Parquet: row-group min/max statistics then become tight, and later filters skip far more data.
concepts.code:
import duckdb, os, tempfile

os.chdir(tempfile.mkdtemp())
con = duckdb.connect()
con.sql("CREATE TABLE t AS SELECT i AS id, 'item' || i AS name FROM range(5) r(i)")

con.sql("COPY t TO 'items.csv' (HEADER, DELIMITER ',')")
con.sql("COPY (SELECT * FROM t WHERE id >= 3 ORDER BY id) TO 'items.parquet' "
        "(FORMAT parquet, COMPRESSION zstd)")

print(open("items.csv").read().splitlines()[:2])   # ['id,name', '0,item0']
print(con.sql("FROM 'items.parquet'").fetchall())  # [(3, 'item3'), (4, 'item4')]
takeaways: `COPY (query) TO 'file'` exports any result; the format follows the file name's ending or FORMAT
`PARTITION_BY` writes Hive-partitioned folders
Sorting before writing Parquet makes later filtering much faster
pitfalls: Writing a partitioned export twice into the same folder without OVERWRITE options and getting an error or duplicate files.

quiz.q: What is the simplest way to convert raw.csv into Parquet with DuckDB?
quiz.explain: COPY writes the result of the inner query (reading the CSV) to a Parquet file.

concepts.name: SQL on pandas, Polars and Arrow
concepts.summary: Query DataFrames by their variable name and get results back as pandas, Polars or Arrow without copying rows.
concepts.why: Mixing SQL and DataFrames lets you use whichever is clearer for each step, and it is often much faster than pandas.
concepts.body:
Python programs often hold tables in a **DataFrame**: a table kept in the program's memory, made with the pandas or Polars libraries. **Arrow** is a related standard way to hold tables in memory, column by column.

DuckDB can query any of these just by using the **variable** it is stored in, meaning the name the Python program gave it: `duckdb.sql("SELECT * FROM df WHERE x > 1")`. This is called a **replacement scan**: if a table name is not found in the database, DuckDB looks for a Python variable with that name.

Results convert back just as easily:

- `.df()` returns a pandas DataFrame
- `.pl()` returns a Polars DataFrame
- `.arrow()` returns an Arrow table

Arrow and Polars data is read with almost no copying, and pandas number columns are read in place. That makes DuckDB a great speed-up for heavy pandas steps: complex joins, grouping by many columns, or running totals and rankings (window functions) are often several times faster and use less memory as SQL.

To save a DataFrame as a database table, run `con.execute("CREATE TABLE t AS SELECT * FROM df")`. Use `con.register("name", df)` to give a DataFrame an explicit name, which you need when the variable isn't visible where the query runs, e.g. it was made inside another function.

Watch types where the two meet: pandas text columns become VARCHAR, timestamps with a time zone become `TIMESTAMP WITH TIME ZONE`, and **NaN** ("not a number", which pandas uses for missing decimal numbers) is not the same as SQL NULL.
concepts.code:
import duckdb
import pandas as pd

orders = pd.DataFrame({"user": ["a", "b", "a", "c"], "amount": [10, 5, 7, 3]})
users = pd.DataFrame({"user": ["a", "b", "c"], "country": ["AM", "FR", "AM"]})

result = duckdb.sql("""
    SELECT u.country, sum(o.amount) AS total
    FROM orders o JOIN users u USING (user)
    GROUP BY ALL ORDER BY total DESC
""").df()                       # back to pandas
print(result.to_dict("list"))
# {'country': ['AM', 'FR'], 'total': [20.0, 5.0]}
takeaways: Name a DataFrame or Arrow table in FROM and DuckDB reads it in place
`.df()`, `.pl()`, `.arrow()` convert results back
Use `con.register` when the DataFrame isn't a variable the query can see
pitfalls: Expecting NaN in a pandas decimal column to behave like SQL NULL in filters and aggregates.

quiz.q: How does DuckDB find `df` in `duckdb.sql('SELECT * FROM df')` when no table df exists?
options: A replacement scan looks up a Python variable named df
It raises an error every time
It downloads the table from a server
quiz.explain: Unknown table names fall back to Python variables with that name, such as DataFrames and Arrow tables.

concepts.name: Lists, structs and maps
concepts.summary: Store and query nested data with LIST, STRUCT and MAP types, unnest them, and transform lists with lambdas.
concepts.why: Data files, especially JSON, often hold lists and records inside records, and DuckDB can work with them without flattening everything first.
concepts.body:
DuckDB has first-class **nested types**, column types that hold several values in one cell:

- `LIST` (e.g. `INTEGER[]`): an ordered list of any length, written `[1, 2, 3]`; positions start at 1, `l[1]`
- `STRUCT`: a **struct** is a small record of named fields, written `{'name': 'Ann', 'age': 34}`; read a field with `s.name` or `s['name']`
- `MAP`: pairs of keys and values, all keys of one type and all values of one type; `MAP {'a': 1}`; `m['a']`
- `ARRAY` (e.g. `FLOAT[3]`): lists of a fixed length, such as three numbers for a point in space

`unnest(list)` turns a list into rows; `unnest(struct)` turns fields into columns, and `unnest(..., recursive := true)` flattens deeply. Going the other way, `list(x)` (also called `array_agg`) collects rows into a list, and `struct_pack` builds structs.

List functions avoid unnesting entirely: `len`, `list_contains`, `list_sort`, `list_distinct`. Some take a small inline function, a **lambda**: `x -> x * 2` means "take x, give back x times 2". `list_transform(l, x -> x * 2)` applies it to each element, `list_filter(l, x -> x > 0)` keeps the elements where it is true, and `list_reduce` combines them. There is even a Python-style shortcut: `[x * 2 FOR x IN l IF x > 0]`.

**JSON** files hold records of names and values in curly braces, often nested. Reading them with `read_json` produces structs and lists automatically, so `SELECT payload.user.id FROM 'events.json'` works out of the box.

Recent versions also accept a Python-style lambda, `lambda x: x * 2`; the arrow form still works, but newer releases may warn that it is on its way out.
concepts.code:
import duckdb

duckdb.sql("""
    CREATE TABLE posts AS SELECT * FROM (VALUES
        (1, ['sql', 'duckdb'], {'name': 'Ann', 'age': 34}),
        (2, ['python'],        {'name': 'Bob', 'age': 19})) t(id, tags, author)
""")
print(duckdb.sql("SELECT id, author.name, len(tags) FROM posts").fetchall())
# [(1, 'Ann', 2), (2, 'Bob', 1)]
print(duckdb.sql("SELECT id, unnest(tags) AS tag FROM posts ORDER BY ALL").fetchall())
# [(1, 'duckdb'), (1, 'sql'), (2, 'python')]
print(duckdb.sql("SELECT [upper(t) FOR t IN tags IF t != 'sql'] FROM posts").fetchall())
# [(['DUCKDB'],), (['PYTHON'],)]
takeaways: `LIST`, `STRUCT`, `MAP` and `ARRAY` are native column types
`unnest` expands lists to rows; `list()` collects rows into a list
Lambdas and the `[x FOR x IN l]` form change lists without unnesting
List positions start at 1
pitfalls: Counting positions from 0 out of habit from other languages: `l[0]` is not the first element.

quiz.explain: unnest turns each list element into its own row.
DuckDB lists are 1-indexed, like SQL arrays in PostgreSQL.

concepts.name: QUALIFY, ASOF joins and PIVOT
concepts.summary: Use DuckDB's analytics features: filter window results with QUALIFY, match readings over time with ASOF JOIN, reshape with PIVOT.
concepts.why: These features turn awkward multi-step queries (top-N per group, nearest timestamp, wide reports) into one clear statement.
concepts.body:
**QUALIFY** filters on window function results the way HAVING filters on aggregates. The classic top-N-per-group query no longer needs a subquery:

```sql
SELECT * FROM sales
QUALIFY row_number() OVER (PARTITION BY region ORDER BY amount DESC) <= 3;
```

**ASOF JOIN** matches each row to the closest preceding row in another table, which is exactly what data recorded over time needs: attach the latest known price to each trade, or the latest config to each event. Write `ASOF JOIN prices p ON t.symbol = p.symbol AND t.ts >= p.ts`. The inequality must be one of `>=`, `>`, `<=`, `<`, and every left row gets at most one match (use `ASOF LEFT JOIN` to keep rows with none).

**PIVOT** turns the distinct values of one column into columns of their own, making a long table wide: `PIVOT sales ON year USING sum(amount) GROUP BY region`. DuckDB discovers the values for you, though listing them (`ON year IN (2024, 2025)`) makes the output columns predictable. **UNPIVOT** does the reverse, folding columns into name/value rows: `UNPIVOT wide ON COLUMNS(* EXCLUDE id) INTO NAME month VALUE amount`.

All three are turned into ordinary query steps inside DuckDB, so they are fast, and they combine freely with CTEs and window functions.
concepts.code:
import duckdb

duckdb.sql("""CREATE TABLE prices AS SELECT * FROM (VALUES
    ('X', 1, 10), ('X', 5, 11), ('X', 9, 12)) t(sym, ts, price)""")
duckdb.sql("""CREATE TABLE trades AS SELECT * FROM (VALUES
    ('X', 4, 100), ('X', 7, 50), ('X', 9, 20)) t(sym, ts, qty)""")

print(duckdb.sql("""
    SELECT t.ts, t.qty, p.price FROM trades t
    ASOF JOIN prices p ON t.sym = p.sym AND t.ts >= p.ts ORDER BY t.ts
""").fetchall())  # [(4, 100, 10), (7, 50, 11), (9, 20, 12)]

print(duckdb.sql("""
    SELECT ts, qty FROM trades
    QUALIFY row_number() OVER (ORDER BY qty DESC) = 1
""").fetchall())  # [(4, 100)]
print(duckdb.sql("PIVOT trades ON ts IN (4, 7) USING sum(qty) GROUP BY sym").fetchall())
# [('X', 100, 50)]
takeaways: QUALIFY filters rows by window function results
ASOF JOIN attaches the nearest preceding match, ideal for data recorded over time
PIVOT/UNPIVOT reshape between long and wide; list the values for predictable columns
pitfalls: Expecting an ASOF JOIN to return several matches per row; it returns at most the single closest one.

quiz.q: A trade at ts=7 is ASOF-joined to prices at ts 1, 5 and 9 with t.ts >= p.ts. Which price row matches?
quiz.explain: ASOF picks the closest row satisfying the inequality: the latest price at or before 7, which is ts=5.

concepts.name: Extensions, S3 and other databases
concepts.summary: Install extensions to read files on S3 and the web, attach PostgreSQL, MySQL or SQLite, and add maps, text search and more.
concepts.why: Extensions let DuckDB query data where it lives, which removes whole export-and-load steps.
concepts.body:
Much of DuckDB's functionality ships as **extensions**: add-ons you turn on with `INSTALL name; LOAD name;`. Official extensions are signed, downloaded once from DuckDB's own server and kept on your computer. Many (like `httpfs`, `json`, `parquet`) **autoload** the first time you use a feature that needs them. `SELECT * FROM duckdb_extensions()` lists what is installed and loaded.

The most used ones:

- `httpfs`: read and write files at `https://` addresses and in online file stores: `s3://` for Amazon S3, `gcs://` for Google's file store, and Azure's.

Those stores need **credentials**: secret keys that prove who you are. DuckDB keeps them as secrets: `CREATE SECRET (TYPE s3, PROVIDER credential_chain)` picks up the keys your Amazon tools already use, or you give `KEY_ID`/`SECRET`/`REGION` yourself. Add `PERSISTENT` to keep the secret for next time.

- `postgres`, `mysql`, `sqlite`: `ATTACH 'dbname=shop host=...' AS pg (TYPE postgres)` makes that database's tables usable in DuckDB; you can join them with local Parquet files and even write back.
- `iceberg` and `delta`: read Iceberg and Delta Lake tables, two popular ways of storing a large table as a folder of Parquet files.
- `spatial` (maps and shapes), `fts` (searching the words in text), `excel`, `vss` (quickly finding the most similar items, stored as lists of numbers).

Community extensions are installed with `INSTALL name FROM community`. Extensions are **native code**: programs that run directly on your computer with full access. So only load ones you trust; settings like `allow_community_extensions` and `autoinstall_known_extensions` let you lock this down on the computers your app runs on.
takeaways: `INSTALL` downloads once; `LOAD` activates; many core extensions autoload
`CREATE SECRET` stores the credentials for S3, Google and Azure file stores
`ATTACH ... (TYPE postgres|mysql|sqlite)` queries other databases in place
pitfalls: Pulling an entire remote PostgreSQL table into DuckDB when a filter could have run in PostgreSQL first; check EXPLAIN.

quiz.q: What is the role of CREATE SECRET when reading s3:// paths?
options: It supplies credentials and region for the S3 requests
It creates a new S3 bucket
quiz.explain: Secrets hold the credentials DuckDB sends to prove who is asking for the remote files.

concepts.name: Vectorized execution and tuning
concepts.summary: How DuckDB runs queries (chunks of column values, many threads, spilling to disk), how to read EXPLAIN ANALYZE and how to tune memory and threads.
concepts.why: Knowing the engine explains performance surprises and lets you handle data bigger than the computer's memory reliably.
concepts.body:
DuckDB executes queries with a **vectorized, push-based** engine. Each step of a query plan (an operator, such as a scan, filter or join) works on **vectors**: chunks of up to 2048 values of one column at a time, which each step pushes on to the next. Chunks this size fit in the CPU's small, very fast built-in memory (its **cache**), and the engine pays its fixed bookkeeping cost once per chunk instead of once per row.

The work is spread over **threads**, separate lines of work running at the same time, normally one per CPU core. This **parallelism** is **morsel-driven**: the input is cut into small chunks (morsels; for Parquet, roughly one row group each), and each thread grabs the next free chunk as soon as it is done, so all cores stay busy.

`EXPLAIN` shows the physical plan; `EXPLAIN ANALYZE` runs the query and labels each operator with its time and row counts. Look for where rows explode (a bad join), which scan dominates, and whether filters and the list of needed columns were pushed into the scan.

Key settings:

- `SET threads = 8;` defaults to the number of cores
- `SET memory_limit = '4GB';` defaults to 80% of the computer's memory
- `SET temp_directory = '/fast/disk';` where spilled data goes

A **hash join** loads one side of a join into a lookup table in memory and checks the other side's rows against it. Hash joins, aggregations, sorts and window functions can **spill to disk** when they exceed the memory limit, so queries larger than memory usually finish, just slower. `preserve_insertion_order = false` lets DuckDB skip ordering work and use less memory on big exports.

Performance tips: prefer Parquet over CSV, keep row groups large, avoid many tiny files, and remember that some operators, such as very large `list()` aggregates, cannot spill.
concepts.code:
import duckdb

con = duckdb.connect()
con.sql("SET threads = 4")
con.sql("SET memory_limit = '1GB'")
con.sql("CREATE TABLE t AS SELECT i, i % 100 AS g FROM range(2_000_000) r(i)")

plan = con.sql("""
    EXPLAIN ANALYZE SELECT g, count(*) FROM t WHERE i % 2 = 0 GROUP BY g
""").fetchall()[0][1]
print("HASH_GROUP_BY" in plan, "Filters:" in plan)  # True True
# the WHERE clause was pushed down into the table scan
print(con.sql("SELECT current_setting('threads')").fetchone())   # (4,)
takeaways: Operators work on column vectors of up to 2048 values
Morsel-driven parallelism keeps every thread busy
`EXPLAIN ANALYZE` shows per-operator time and row counts
`memory_limit` and `temp_directory` control spilling for queries bigger than memory
pitfalls: Setting memory_limit close to the computer's total memory while other programs also run there; the system may then kill DuckDB for using too much.

quiz.q: A GROUP BY needs more memory than memory_limit allows. What does DuckDB typically do?
options: Spill intermediate state to the temp directory and continue
quiz.explain: Joins, aggregates and sorts are designed to offload to disk when they exceed the memory budget.

concepts.name: Storage format and concurrency
concepts.summary: Inside the .duckdb file: row groups, compression, zone maps, MVCC transactions and the one-writer rule.
concepts.why: Designing an app around DuckDB requires knowing what it guarantees when several users or threads work at once, and how data is laid out.
concepts.body:
A DuckDB database file is split into fixed-size blocks. Tables are stored as **row groups** of about 122,880 rows. Inside each, every column is a separate **column segment**, compressed in a way picked to suit its values: for example a run of identical values stored once, or **dictionary encoding**, which keeps each distinct value once plus small numbers pointing to it.

Each segment also keeps its min/max values, called **zone maps**, so filters skip segments that cannot match. That is why inserting data sorted by a common filter column speeds up queries.

Indexes are rarely needed: zone maps cover range filters. PRIMARY KEY and UNIQUE constraints create **ART** indexes (a tree-shaped index), which help look up single rows but slow bulk loads.

Changes go first to a **write-ahead log** (WAL): a separate file where each change is recorded before it is applied, so nothing is lost if the program crashes. They are copied into the main file at a **checkpoint**, automatically once the WAL grows past `checkpoint_threshold`, or when you run `CHECKPOINT`. Freed space is reused, but the file rarely shrinks.

Transactions use **MVCC** (multi-version concurrency control): a change creates a new version of a row instead of overwriting it, so each transaction keeps seeing a **snapshot** of the data as it was when it started. Within one program many threads can read and write in parallel; if two transactions change the same row, the second fails to commit.

Across programs the rule is strict: **either one process opens the file read-write, or any number open it read-only** (`read_only=True`). A **process** is one running program. For many writers, send all writes through one process, use a server database, or use setups built for it such as DuckLake or MotherDuck.
concepts.code:
import duckdb, os, tempfile

path = os.path.join(tempfile.mkdtemp(), "app.duckdb")
con = duckdb.connect(path)
con.sql("CREATE TABLE t AS SELECT i FROM range(300_000) r(i)")
con.sql("CHECKPOINT")
print(con.sql("""SELECT count(DISTINCT row_group_id)
                 FROM pragma_storage_info('t')""").fetchone())   # (3,)
con.close()

ro1 = duckdb.connect(path, read_only=True)    # many read-only handles are fine
print(ro1.sql("SELECT max(i) FROM t").fetchone())   # (299999,)
takeaways: Tables are row groups of ~122k rows, each column compressed separately
Zone maps (min/max) let scans skip data, so sort on common filter columns
MVCC gives each transaction a snapshot within one process; conflicting updates fail
One read-write process or many read-only processes per file
pitfalls: Opening the same file read-write from several copies of a website's server program at once; all but the first get a lock error.

quiz.q: Two separate Python processes need to write to the same .duckdb file. What happens?
options: Writes are merged at the next checkpoint
The second process fails to acquire the file lock
quiz.explain: MVCC works between threads in one process; across processes only one may open the file for writing.

concepts.name: How the optimizer rewrites queries
concepts.summary: See what DuckDB's optimizer does to your SQL: pushdown, join ordering, build-side choice, Top-N and statistics propagation.
concepts.why: Reading optimized plans tells you when a query is slow because of your SQL and when the engine already fixed it for you.
concepts.body:
Before execution, DuckDB's **optimizer** rewrites the logical plan in a series of passes. The ones that matter most in practice:

- **Filter pushdown**: WHERE conditions move as low as possible, into joins and into the scan itself, where zone maps or Parquet statistics can skip data. Filters on one side of a join are also copied to the other side when the join key makes them equivalent.
- **Projection pushdown**: only referenced columns are read. `SELECT *` on a Parquet file with many columns costs real reading time.
- **Join ordering**: a cost-based join-order optimizer uses row-count estimates (from table statistics and distinct counts) to choose the order of multi-way joins and, for hash joins, puts the smaller input on the **build side**.
- **Top-N**: `ORDER BY ... LIMIT n` becomes a TOP_N operator that keeps only the best n rows seen so far instead of sorting everything.
- **Statistics propagation**: known min/max values flow through expressions, letting DuckDB remove impossible filters, group small whole-number ranges with a simple direct lookup, and store in-between results in smaller number types.
- **Common subexpression and CTE handling**: CTEs referenced several times may be materialized once.

`EXPLAIN` shows the optimized physical plan with estimated row counts (`~rows`). When estimates are far from actual counts in `EXPLAIN ANALYZE`, the join order may be poor; rewriting the query, adding a filter earlier or materializing an intermediate table can help. `SET disabled_optimizers = '...'` exists for tracking down problems, not for everyday use.
concepts.code:
import duckdb

con = duckdb.connect()
con.sql("CREATE TABLE users AS SELECT i AS id, i % 50 AS country FROM range(100000) r(i)")
con.sql("CREATE TABLE events AS SELECT i % 100000 AS user_id FROM range(1000000) r(i)")

plan = con.sql("""
    EXPLAIN SELECT u.country, count(*) AS n
    FROM events e JOIN users u ON e.user_id = u.id
    WHERE u.country = 3
    GROUP BY ALL ORDER BY n DESC LIMIT 5
""").fetchall()[0][1]

print("TOP_N" in plan)                # True   sort + limit became Top-N
print("Filters: country=3" in plan)   # True   filter pushed into the users scan
print("HASH_JOIN" in plan)            # True
takeaways: Filters and projections are pushed down into scans automatically
Join order and build side come from row-count estimates
ORDER BY + LIMIT becomes a cheap Top-N operator
Compare estimated (~rows) with actual counts to spot bad plans
pitfalls: Hand-optimizing join order in SQL text; DuckDB reorders inner joins anyway, so fix estimates or filters instead.

quiz.q: Why does DuckDB normally put the smaller table on the build side of a hash join?
options: The build side is always read from disk twice
The lookup table is built from the build side, so a smaller one uses less memory and builds faster
SQL requires the smaller table to be written first
Only the build side can have filters
quiz.explain: The lookup table holds the build input, so building from the smaller input is cheaper in time and memory.
